title: The Choctaw Gift to Starving Ireland
text:
In the early 1830s the United States government forced the Choctaw Nation off its homelands in Mississippi and marched its people west to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma. Thousands died of exposure, hunger and disease on the way, on one of the routes later remembered as the Trail of Tears.

Fifteen years later, news reached them of another catastrophe. In Ireland the potato crop had failed again and again, and hundreds of thousands of people were dying of hunger and disease. In March 1847 Choctaw people gathered at a meeting in Skullyville, in Indian Territory, and took up a collection for Irish famine relief. They raised 170 dollars, a considerable sum for a community that had little, and sent it on through a relief committee.

The gift was reported in American newspapers at the time and then largely forgotten outside the two peoples. In Ireland it was never fully forgotten. In 2017 the town of Midleton in County Cork unveiled a large steel sculpture called Kindred Spirits, a ring of tall eagle feathers, to honor the Choctaw donation, and Irish leaders, among them President Mary Robinson in 1995, have visited the Choctaw Nation to give thanks.
lesson: Those who have suffered can be the quickest to recognize suffering in others. Giving from little, to strangers far away, creates bonds that last generations.
source: Arkansas Intelligencer and other contemporary American newspaper reports (1847); records of famine relief committees
